title: The Taped Knuckle
passages:
"No," Kass said, into the set, and loud enough that the open channel carried it up the ore line to Anza's board and out onto the morning desk's relief overflow, where it would sit in a log until somebody with a clean record read it. "Nobody signs anything. Not on my channel."

"Dispatcher," Marlowe said. His voice came through the pump bulb — the old brass horn bolted above the door, spliced into the set at some point before either of them was born — thin but clear, with a splinted man's careful breathing behind it. "You clear loads. You don't clear me."

"It's a trade, not a load."

"It's my body, and I outrank you on it. Desk can requisition cargo. Nobody requisitions a man's ribs but the man." A pause, a wet cough, then: "Kass. Sign it. I've had worse Tuesdays."

Under his voice, faint, a squeak of rubber on a hand pump, in and out, patient as a metronome. Then Rhea, close to the bulb, none of the patience in her voice at all.

"Kass. Take the deal."

"Rhea—"

"Four restarts left. Four. After that I'm squeezing the bag with my hands for however long it takes you to walk back up that grade, and my arm is already gone from the shoulder down." Inhale, squeak, exhale. "I don't want Voss. I want what's on that puck. A reseal carries a time. Get me the time off the sender, get me the six cases, put the scrubbers on a rig. That's all I'm asking."

"The time tells us who shut it," Kass said. "Not whether Voss tells the truth about the rest."

"Nobody's feeding anything," Voss said, from the bench. He had the flat, unbothered look of a man who'd erased himself so thoroughly that weather had more claim on him than people did. "You've got twenty minutes of daylight and a reclaimer with a clearance that turns before eight. Sign, and the scrubbers are yours by seven."

Kass looked at the stack. Eleven cases, Anza's marks on every one, corded and pucked, sitting on a dead pump station's floor like they'd been raised there.

"I want to look at one."

"Nothing in here is free," Brill said. She had her lamp in one hand, a kerosene thing with a cracked chimney, and she held it the way other people hold a wrench. "Not even the light."

"Ospina," Kass said. "What does your ring buy in this room?"

Ospina had been standing with their coat still on, the dirty mark on their authority sitting there like a stain nobody could see but everybody could price. They put their hand out flat. "A receiving counter. Her stock reads Bay 4 sent and Culvert Nine received, in her own ledger, in her own hall. It stops being stolen."

Brill's chin came up. "It also puts my station's name in a ledger."

"Your winter's already got a name on it," Kass said. "Eleven seals off Anza's down-line. Only question left is whether the name is thief or receiver, and that gets decided at eight either way."

Brill set the lamp on the bench and stepped back, which in that room was a signature.

Ospina lifted the nearest case enough to turn it. The sender puck was a steel disk the size of a thumbnail, crimped over the seal wire on the lid: the only thing on a rig that says who shut it and when. Its face is a shallow strike, meant to be read flat under a powered reader, and the pump station had no power, so there was nothing to do but tilt it into the flame and let the light rake across the metal.

"Talk while they look," Marlowe said, over the bulb.

"Quiet," Kass said. "Ospina. Whose?"

Ospina turned the puck a quarter inch. The strike came up out of the steel in pieces, bright where the metal was cut and dark where it was pressed, and Ospina looked at it for a long enough time that the pump bulb hissed and Rhea's hand went around again at the far end.

Behind them, Miko put one hand flat on the overlap log and kept it there.

"Kass," Ospina said. "Hold the trade."
